title: Britain to get first look at new AI systems after White House U-turn
content:
The White House has reinstated the UK’s access to the latest AI models for safety testing after lobbying from ministers, The Telegraph can reveal.
The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) will now be able to access the latest models from US tech companies before they are released, allowing British officials to run safety tests.
Last month, the White House asked Anthropic, OpenAI and other major AI companies to stop sharing their models with AISI, in a major blow to Andy Burnham’s attempt to become a world leader in AI regulation.
After the order from Donald Trump’s Office of the National Cyber Director, Anthropic restricted UK officials from reviewing its new Claude Mythos 5.1 model.
The Telegraph understands that decision has been reversed after lobbying from Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, and AISI will be given pre-release access to models from Anthropic, Google Deepmind and OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT.
Mr Burnham’s push for international regulation of AI models comes despite Mr Trump’s warning that “globalist” organisations should not interfere with the development of models by American companies.
Mr Trump told the United Nations General Assembly last month that he wanted to “encourage” AI, “not rein it in”.
He said: “Americans have never been a nation that retreats from a frontier or shrinks from a challenge, no matter how great or how daunting that challenge may be.”
Raft of new measures
However, in a speech on Monday, Mr Narayan will warn that tech companies cannot be left to regulate themselves, and will announce a series of new measures to reduce the risk of AI to the Government, companies and the public.
He will announce changes to Labour’s Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which will strengthen the requirement for companies working on critical national infrastructure projects to report to the Government any security breaches using AI.
Ministers are also planning to increase the Government’s use of frontier AI – the most recent and advanced models – to protect Whitehall departments from cyber attacks.
On Sunday, it was reported that the heads of MI6, MI5 and GCHQ had warned ministers that AI had empowered hostile actors and terrorists who could use it to shut down sensitive sites or obtain confidential information.
Mr Narayan will also announce more support from the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) – an offshoot of GCHQ – for companies to defend themselves from AI-powered attacks.
Cybersecurity officials in the NCSC, Cabinet Office and Department for Culture, Media and Sport will be given greater resources to investigate and respond to incidents.
A source said the speech would be a “genuinely significant intervention” on the risks posed by AI companies and their products, while signalling that Britain would defend itself using AI where necessary.
Britain has attempted to pitch itself as a global leader on AI regulation through the AISI, which is more advanced than its international competitors.
Mr Burnham said during his speech to the UN that Britain would use its presidency of the G20 next year to press for further global collaboration on AI.

report.summary: The White House has reversed its block, restoring UK AI Security Institute pre-release access to frontier models from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI for safety testing.
report.background: The White House initially told Anthropic, OpenAI and other US labs to stop giving the UK's AI Security Institute pre-release model access, a blow to Britain's ambition to lead global AI regulation. The order followed Trump administration skepticism of 'globalist' AI rules, and Anthropic restricted UK review of Claude Mythos 5.1. After lobbying by AI minister Kanishka Narayan, the decision was reversed, restoring access for AISI to test frontier models from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI. The episode highlights growing tension between US deregulation and UK/European safety testing, as well as mounting cyber concerns from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ.
key_points: The White House reversed its earlier order, so the UK AI Security Institute can again review new models from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI before public release. The change came after lobbying by UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan, following a period when Anthropic blocked UK officials from examining its Claude Mythos 5.1 model.

In a Monday speech, Narayan will reject self-regulation by tech firms and announce changes to Labour's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill. Critical national infrastructure companies would face stronger duties to report AI-related security breaches to government. Ministers also plan to expand Whitehall's use of frontier AI to defend against cyber attacks.

UK security chiefs from MI5, MI6 and GCHQ have warned ministers that AI gives hostile actors and terrorists new power to shut down sensitive sites or steal confidential data. The National Cyber Security Centre will receive more support and resources to help companies defend against AI-powered attacks and investigate incidents.

Britain is positioning itself as a global AI regulation leader, using the AISI and its upcoming G20 presidency to push international collaboration. This contrasts with Donald Trump's UN warning that 'globalist' bodies should not interfere with US AI development; he said he wants to encourage AI, not rein it in.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the U-turn signals that pre-release safety testing for trusted governments may become a de facto condition for operating in key markets, even amid US deregulatory rhetoric. US labs such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind must balance commercial speed with UK and allied scrutiny, potentially adding review steps and documentation. Developers may see more standardized evaluations, reporting duties and security expectations, especially for critical infrastructure. Regular users could benefit from safer, better-vetted models and stronger cyber defenses, but may also face slower releases, more government oversight, and regional differences in model availability and features.
report.tools: To follow this space, watch the UK AISI's open-source Inspect evaluation framework, METR's autonomous capability evaluations, Garak for LLM vulnerability scanning, Microsoft's PyRIT, and Cybench cybersecurity benchmarks. Also track NCSC guidance, the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill text, and system cards from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind. These help developers and researchers replicate safety testing, red-teaming, and compliance checks.
